english: to be quick to read the room / perceptive about how others feel (lit. 'one's nunchi is fast')
usage: 걔는 눈치가 빨라서 같이 일하기 편해.
He's quick to read the room, so he's easy to work with.
Praising a coworker/friend
눈치가 빠른 사람은 분위기를 금방 파악해요.
Perceptive people pick up on the mood right away.
General statement, polite
눈치 좀 챙겨.
Read the room a little.
눈치(를) 챙기다/보다 — telling someone to be more aware
나 눈치 없어서 분위기 다 깼잖아.
I'm so oblivious I totally killed the mood.
눈치 없다 = the opposite; self-deprecating
examples: 사장님 표정 보고 눈치가 빨라서 바로 조용히 했어.
He read the boss's face fast and went quiet right away.
Reacting to an unspoken signal
눈치가 빠른 편이라 친구 기분 나쁜 거 금방 알아챘어요.
I'm fairly perceptive, so I quickly noticed my friend was upset.
눈치가 빠른 편 = 'on the perceptive side'
여기선 눈치가 빨라야 살아남아요.
Around here you have to be quick on the uptake to survive.
Office/social-survival nuance
nuance: 눈치 is the Korean social radar for reading unspoken cues, and 빠르다 ('fast') means you catch them quickly — so it's a compliment for being tactful and socially sharp. Casual-to-polite; common at work and among friends. The flip side 눈치(가) 없다 ('no nunchi') means clueless or oblivious, and 눈치(를) 보다 means to anxiously watch someone's mood.
mistakes: Don't translate it literally as 'fast eyes' — 눈치 is social awareness, not eyesight.
눈치가 빠르다 (perceptive) ≠ 눈치를 보다 (to nervously gauge someone's reaction); they're different and not interchangeable.

english: to be well-connected / know a lot of people (lit. 'one's feet are wide')
usage: 걔 진짜 발 넓어, 모르는 사람이 없어.
She's so well-connected — there's nobody she doesn't know.
Casual, about a friend
발이 넓으셔서 소개를 많이 받으시겠어요.
You know so many people, you must get a lot of introductions.
Polite, to an older/senior person
발 넓은 친구한테 부탁하면 금방 구할 거야.
If you ask that connected friend, you'll find it fast.
Using someone's network
나는 발이 좁아서 아는 사람이 별로 없어.
I don't have many connections, so I barely know anyone.
발이 좁다 = the opposite
examples: 발이 넓어서 어느 동네를 가도 아는 사람을 만나요.
He's so well-connected he runs into someone he knows in any neighborhood.
Describing a social hub
일자리 알아보는 거면 발 넓은 선배한테 물어봐.
If you're job-hunting, ask that senior who knows everyone.
Tapping a network for jobs
발이 넓은 게 사회생활에선 큰 장점이에요.
Being well-connected is a big advantage in professional life.
사회생활 = work/social life
nuance: Literally 'wide feet,' but it means having a broad social network — lots of acquaintances across many circles. It's a compliment about someone's connections, not their popularity or closeness. Neutral register; works in both casual and polite speech. Note it's about breadth of contacts, not how deep the friendships are.
mistakes: Nothing to do with foot size — never read it literally.
It describes breadth of acquaintances, not having many close friends; don't use it to mean 'has lots of best friends.'

english: to be generous / cook or give in large quantities (lit. 'one's hands are big')
usage: 엄마가 손이 커서 명절마다 음식이 넘쳐나.
Mom cooks in such big batches that there's a flood of food every holiday.
Classic use — about cooking amounts
사장님이 손이 크셔서 회식 때 많이 사 주세요.
The boss is generous, so he treats us a lot at company dinners.
Polite, about spending freely
손 크게 좀 준비했어, 많이 먹어.
I made a generous spread — eat up.
손 크게 = 'generously / in big quantity'
난 손이 작아서 늘 모자라게 사.
I always under-buy because I tend to skimp.
손이 작다 = the opposite (stingy/small portions)
examples: 할머니는 손이 커서 한 번 끓이면 동네 사람들 다 먹어요.
Grandma cooks so big that when she makes a pot, the whole neighborhood eats.
About cooking volume
손이 크신 분이라 선물도 늘 푸짐해요.
She's generous, so her gifts are always lavish.
Generosity with gifts/spending
오늘 손 크게 쐈으니까 다음엔 네가 사.
I splurged today, so next time it's on you.
Treating people generously
nuance: Literally 'big hands,' it praises generosity — especially making lots of food or spending freely on others. It often carries a warm, hospitable feel (Korean food culture loves abundance). Neutral-to-positive register. The opposite, 손이 작다 ('small hands'), means stingy or always preparing too little.
mistakes: Not about literal hand size or being a big spender on yourself — it's about generosity toward others.
Don't confuse it with 손이 빠르다 ('fast hands' = efficient/quick worker), which is unrelated.

english: to be tight-lipped / good at keeping secrets (lit. 'one's mouth is heavy')
usage: 걔는 입이 무거우니까 말해도 돼.
He's tight-lipped, so it's fine to tell him.
Reassuring someone a secret is safe
입 무거운 사람한테만 얘기하는 거예요.
I'm only telling someone who can keep a secret.
Polite, setting a confidential tone
걱정 마, 나 입 진짜 무거워.
Don't worry, I really know how to keep quiet.
Promising discretion
쟤는 입이 가벼워서 소문 다 퍼뜨려.
She's a blabbermouth and spreads every rumor.
입이 가볍다 = the opposite
examples: 이건 비밀인데, 너 입 무거운 거 알아서 말하는 거야.
This is a secret, but I'm telling you because I know you're discreet.
Confiding in someone
입이 무거운 직원이라 회사에서 신뢰를 받아요.
He's a discreet employee, so he's trusted at the company.
Workplace virtue
변호사는 기본적으로 입이 무거워야 해요.
A lawyer fundamentally has to be tight-lipped.
Professional discretion
nuance: Literally 'heavy mouth' — it means you don't let words slip easily, i.e. you can be trusted with secrets. It's a compliment, often used to vouch for someone before sharing something private. Neutral register. The opposite, 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth'), means a gossip who can't keep anything quiet.
mistakes: Has nothing to do with being quiet/shy in general — it's specifically about keeping secrets.
Opposite is 입이 가볍다, not 입이 작다; don't mix the body-part idioms up.

english: to be easily swayed / quick to believe what others say (lit. 'one's ears are thin')
usage: 나 귀가 얇아서 광고 보면 자꾸 사.
I'm so easily swayed I keep buying stuff I see in ads.
Self-deprecating, about shopping
귀가 얇으시네요, 그 말을 다 믿으세요?
You're easily persuaded — you believe all that?
Polite-ish, gently teasing
걔 귀 얇아서 누가 꼬시면 바로 넘어가.
He's a pushover — anyone can talk him into it.
넘어가다 = to be won over
귀 얇은 사람은 사기당하기 쉬워요.
Gullible people are easy to scam.
Cautionary
examples: 친구가 좋다고 하니까 귀가 얇아져서 같은 걸 샀어.
My friend said it was good, and I caved and bought the same thing.
Influenced by a recommendation
주식도 귀가 얇으면 남 말 듣고 손해 봐요.
With stocks too, if you're easily swayed you lose money following others.
Financial warning
내가 귀가 얇은 편이라 결정할 때 조심하려고 해.
I'm on the gullible side, so I try to be careful when deciding.
귀가 얇은 편 = 'somewhat easily swayed'
nuance: Literally 'thin ears,' it describes someone who's easily persuaded or quick to believe whatever they hear — gullible or impressionable. Usually mildly negative or self-mocking, not a harsh insult. Casual-to-polite. Think of thin ears as letting sound (and influence) pass right through.
mistakes: Not about hearing ability or thin physical ears — it's about being easily influenced.
It implies gullibility, not open-mindedness; don't use it as a compliment for being flexible.

english: to get stood up (when someone fails to show for a date/meeting) (lit. 'to be hit by the wind')
usage: 나 어제 소개팅에서 바람맞았어.
I got stood up on my blind date yesterday.
바람맞다 often written as one word
한 시간 기다리다가 결국 바람맞았어요.
I waited an hour and ended up getting stood up.
Polite, recounting
또 바람맞히면 진짜 화낼 거야.
If you stand me up again I'll really be mad.
바람(을) 맞히다 = to stand someone up (causative)
걔가 날 바람맞혔어.
She stood me up.
Subject is the one who didn't show
examples: 카페에서 두 시간 기다렸는데 바람맞았어.
I waited two hours at the cafe and got stood up.
Classic stood-up scene
연락도 없이 바람맞히는 건 진짜 예의가 아니야.
Standing someone up without even a text is just rude.
Complaining about the behavior
거래처가 미팅에 안 나와서 바람맞은 기분이에요.
The client didn't show for the meeting, so I feel stood up.
Extended to a business no-show
nuance: Literally 'to be hit by wind,' it means the person you were supposed to meet never showed — you got stood up. Most common for dates and 소개팅 (blind dates) but also used for any no-show. Casual register. Watch the pair: 바람(을) 맞다 = you got stood up; 바람(을) 맞히다 = you stood someone else up.
mistakes: Don't confuse with 바람(을) 피우다, which means to cheat on a partner — completely different.
바람맞다 (got stood up) vs 바람맞히다 (stood someone up): mixing these reverses who's at fault.

english: to lose track of time / not notice time passing (because you're absorbed/having fun)
usage: 너랑 얘기하다 보면 시간 가는 줄 모르겠어.
When I'm talking with you I lose all track of time.
Sweet/casual
게임하느라 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
I lost track of time playing games.
Polite, explaining lateness
책이 재밌어서 시간 가는 줄도 몰랐어.
The book was so good I didn't even notice the time.
줄도 adds emphasis
수다 떨다가 시간 가는 줄 모르고 막차 놓쳤어.
We were chatting and lost track of time and missed the last train.
Common consequence
examples: 오랜만에 친구 만나서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
I met a friend after ages and totally lost track of time.
Catching up
일에 집중하다 보면 시간 가는 줄 몰라요.
When I get absorbed in work, time just flies by.
Being in flow
여기 너무 재밌어서 다들 시간 가는 줄 몰랐대.
Everyone said this place was so fun they lost track of time.
Reported, about an outing
nuance: Literally 'to not know that time is going,' it means you were so absorbed or enjoying yourself that you didn't notice time passing — time flew. Warm, positive feel; great for explaining why you stayed late or were late. Casual-to-polite. It's about pleasant absorption, not carelessness.
mistakes: Keep the structure 가는 줄 모르다 — beginners drop 줄 and it stops meaning 'didn't realize that…'.
It implies you enjoyed the time, so don't use it as an excuse for laziness or neglecting something important.

english: to have a hard/stressful time / sweat it out (lit. 'to drain greasy sweat')
usage: 면접에서 어려운 질문 받고 진땀 뺐어.
I got a tough question in the interview and was sweating bullets.
진땀 빼다, often without 을
설명하느라 진땀을 뺐어요.
I had a really hard time explaining it.
Polite
애 달래느라 진땀 뺐네.
I sweated it out trying to calm the kid down.
Everyday parenting struggle
고객 항의 받고 진땀 흘렸어.
I broke out in a sweat dealing with the customer complaint.
진땀(을) 흘리다 = close variant
examples: 발표 중에 노트북이 멈춰서 진땀을 뺐어요.
My laptop froze mid-presentation and I was sweating it out.
Stressful work moment
길을 잃어서 한참 헤매며 진땀 뺐어.
I got lost and sweated it out wandering for ages.
Stressful situation
통역하느라 진땀 뺐는데 그래도 잘 끝났어요.
I had a stressful time interpreting, but it ended well.
Hard task that worked out
nuance: 진땀 is the clammy 'cold sweat' you break into under pressure, so 진땀을 빼다 means to struggle through something nerve-wracking or exhausting. It captures the flustered, scrambling feeling, not just physical effort. Casual-to-polite. 진땀(을) 흘리다 ('to shed cold sweat') is a near-synonym you'll hear just as often.
mistakes: Don't read it as literal sweating from heat or exercise — it's about stress and struggle.
It's 진땀 (clammy stress-sweat), a specific word — not just 땀 (ordinary sweat).

english: to catch one's breath / get a moment's relief after something hectic
usage: 일 끝나고 이제 좀 한숨 돌렸어.
Now that work's done I've finally caught my breath.
Casual, post-rush relief
바쁜 거 끝나서 한숨 돌리고 있어요.
The busy stretch is over so I'm taking a breather.
Polite
이거만 처리하면 한숨 돌릴 수 있어.
Once I handle this I can finally relax a bit.
Anticipating relief
겨우 한숨 돌리나 했더니 또 일이 터졌어.
Just when I thought I could breathe, another problem blew up.
Common 'no rest' pattern
examples: 이사 다 끝내고 커피 마시면서 한숨 돌렸어요.
After finishing the move I caught my breath over a coffee.
Relief after a big task
시험 끝났으니까 좀 한숨 돌려.
Exams are over, so take a breather.
Telling someone to relax
급한 불은 껐으니 한숨 돌릴 수 있겠네요.
We put out the worst of it, so we can breathe now.
급한 불 끄다 pairs naturally here
nuance: Literally 'to turn/let out one breath,' it means to finally catch your breath and feel relief once a hectic or stressful stretch eases up. It implies the pressure has just lifted, even if briefly. Casual-to-polite, very common in daily and work life. Often paired with 이제 ('now') or 겨우 ('barely').
mistakes: Don't confuse with 한숨(을) 쉬다, which is to sigh out of worry/frustration — different feeling entirely.
It's about momentary relief after stress, not taking a long vacation or fully resting.

english: for excitement to fizzle / the mood to be killed (lit. 'the steam leaks out')
usage: 기대했는데 취소돼서 김이 새 버렸어.
I was looking forward to it but it got canceled, so the excitement just fizzled.
Casual disappointment
미리 결말 말하지 마, 김새잖아.
Don't spoil the ending — it ruins it.
김새다 = common contracted form
분위기 좋았는데 그 말 한마디에 김이 샜어요.
The mood was nice but that one comment killed it.
Polite, mood deflated
준비 다 했는데 비 와서 김이 팍 샜어.
I had everything ready but the rain totally deflated it.
팍 adds 'suddenly/totally'
examples: 서프라이즈였는데 누가 미리 말해서 김이 다 샜어.
It was a surprise, but someone spilled it and all the excitement was gone.
Spoiled surprise
다들 가기로 했다가 한 명씩 빠지니까 김새네.
Everyone was going to go, then people dropped out one by one — such a buzzkill.
Plans falling apart
열심히 만들었는데 반응이 없어서 좀 김이 샜어요.
I worked hard on it but got no reaction, so I felt kind of deflated.
Effort met with indifference
nuance: Literally 'the steam escapes' (like a deflating 김밥/만두 losing its hot steam), it means built-up excitement or a good mood suddenly goes flat. You say it when something spoils the anticipation — a cancellation, a spoiler, a buzzkill comment. Casual register; 김새다 is the everyday contracted form, and 김(이) 빠지다 means the same thing.
mistakes: Nothing to do with 김 the edible seaweed — here 김 means steam/vapor.
It describes deflated excitement/mood, not literally something leaking; don't use it for actual gas or air leaks.

english: to be anxious/worried sick / eaten up with worry (lit. 'one's insides burn')
usage: 연락이 안 돼서 속이 타 죽겠어.
I can't reach them and I'm worried sick.
Casual, intense worry
합격 발표 기다리느라 속이 타요.
I'm on edge waiting for the results.
Polite, anxious waiting
애가 아픈데 약도 없어서 속이 탔어.
My kid was sick with no medicine, and I was frantic.
Helpless worry
그렇게 속 태우지 말고 좀 기다려 봐.
Don't fret like that — just wait a bit.
속(을) 태우다 = to make someone worry / to fret
examples: 면접 결과를 몰라서 며칠째 속이 타고 있어요.
I don't know the interview result and I've been anxious for days.
Prolonged anxiety
계약이 미뤄질까 봐 속이 탔는데 다행히 잘됐어.
I was stressing that the deal might fall through, but luckily it worked out.
Worry that resolves
부모님은 자식 일이라면 늘 속을 태우세요.
Parents always worry themselves sick over their kids.
속을 태우다 in habitual sense
nuance: Literally 'the insides burn,' it conveys the gnawing, burning anxiety of worrying about something out of your control — waiting on news, an unreachable person, a sick family member. Stronger and more visceral than 걱정하다 ('to worry'). Casual-to-polite. Causative 속(을) 태우다 means to fret, or to make someone else worry.
mistakes: Don't take it literally as heartburn or indigestion — it's emotional anxiety.
속이 타다 = you feel anxious; 속을 태우다 = you cause worry (often to others). Keep the 이/을 distinction.

english: to be jam-packed / so crowded there's no room to step (lit. 'no gap to set a foot')
usage: 주말 명동은 발 디딜 틈이 없어.
Myeongdong on weekends is absolutely packed.
Casual, about a crowded place
행사장이 발 디딜 틈이 없었어요.
The venue was jam-packed.
Polite, past tense
출근 시간 지하철은 발 디딜 틈도 없어요.
The subway at rush hour has no room to even stand.
틈도 없다 adds emphasis
축제라 거리에 발 디딜 틈이 없더라.
It was a festival so the streets were packed solid.
-더라 = reporting what you witnessed
examples: 세일 첫날이라 매장에 발 디딜 틈이 없었어.
It was the first day of the sale, so the store was mobbed.
Crowded shop
벚꽃 축제 때는 공원이 발 디딜 틈이 없어요.
During the cherry blossom festival the park is shoulder to shoulder.
Seasonal crowds
맛집이라 그런지 점심엔 발 디딜 틈이 없네요.
Must be a famous spot — it's packed at lunch.
Popular restaurant
nuance: Literally 'no gap to plant your foot,' it's a vivid way to say a place is so crowded there's nowhere to step. Use it for packed streets, stores, subways, festivals — anywhere overflowing with people. Casual-to-polite. It emphasizes sheer density of a crowd, often with a slightly overwhelmed tone.
mistakes: Spacing matters: 발 디딜 틈이 없다 (발 디딜 = 'to step'), not 발디딜.
It's specifically about crowds of people, not about a room being cluttered with objects.
